chunks: From him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from Muhammad ibn al-Fudayl, from Abu al-Subah al-Kinani, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

When a man performs khul' (divorce by redemption) with his wife, she is one irrevocable divorce, and he is suitor-like among the suitors. It is not permissible for him to take back what he gave until she is the one who requests that from him without him harming her, and until she says: 'I will not be dutiful to you with an oath, nor will I bathe for you from major impurity, and I will surely bring into your house someone you dislike, and I will lie on your bed and not establish God's boundaries.' If this is from her, then what he took from her is pleasing to him.

key_terms.بَائِنٌ: Irrevocable/Severed (referring to the status of the divorce)
key_terms.جَنَابَةٍ: Major ritual impurity (requiring full body wash)
key_terms.خَاطِبٌ: Suitor/Claimant (referring to the husband's right to reclaim)
key_terms.خَلَعَ: Khul' (divorce by redemption where wife pays compensation)

ai.seo_question: What are the specific conditions under which a husband can reclaim the khul' compensation in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In al-Isfahani's narration from Imam al-Sadiq, the condition of 'bainuna' (irrevocability) is established immediately upon the husband's act of khul', distinguishing it from revocable divorce. The Imam specifies that the husband's right to retain the compensation is contingent upon the wife's voluntary initiation and her explicit declaration of intent to cease marital duties, such as intimacy and cohabitation, thereby validating the transaction. This highlights the Shia juristic emphasis on mutual consent and the absence of coercion in financial settlements during divorce.
